Why you can trust it

  • Your password is made on your device. It’s never sent, saved or seen — not even by me.
  • Every character is picked completely at random, so there’s no pattern anyone can guess.
  • Want something you can remember? Switch to Passphrase for a few random words.

How it works

  1. 1Pick a styleRandom characters, easy-to-say words, or a PIN.
  2. 2Set the lengthLonger is stronger — 16+ characters is plenty.
  3. 3Copy and use itIt’s made on your device and never sent anywhere.

How strong is strong enough?

For most accounts, a random password of 16 characters or more is plenty — no one can guess it. A 20-character one from this page would take longer than the age of the universe to crack.

For the few passwords you have to type yourself — like your phone or your password manager — a passphrase of five or six random words is easier to remember and still very strong.

Is anything sent to a server?

No. The password is made inside this page, on your device. You can even turn off your Wi-Fi and it still works.

Why skip look-alike characters?

Letters like l, 1, I, O and 0 are easy to mix up when you read a password out loud or type it by hand. Skipping them makes life easier — just add a couple of characters to keep it strong.

What does “at least one of each” do?

Some websites insist on a number, a capital letter and a symbol. This makes sure every type you picked appears at least once.

For the technical folks

Randomness comes from crypto.getRandomValues with rejection sampling, so there’s no modulo bias. Passphrases use the EFF short wordlist (1,296 words, about 10.3 bits each). A 20-character password from all four sets is about 130 bits.
